entry.title: Arroyo Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Rust SQL Streaming Engine

link.title: Arroyo Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Rust SQL Streaming Engine

entry.content:
Modern machine learning is increasingly a streaming problem. Models that score fraud, rank feeds, or trigger alerts do not want a nightly table dump — they want fresh features computed continuously over the same event streams that drive the product. Arroyo is a distributed stream processing engine written in Rust that attacks exactly this layer: you write SQL, and it performs stateful computations over bounded and unbounded sources, emitting results as soon as they arrive. Its README lists “Real-time ML feature generation” as a first-class use case, alongside fraud detection and real-time ingestion into data lakes.

Why does a streaming engine belong in an AI infrastructure stack? Because feature computation is the connective tissue between raw events and model serving. Rolling counts, per-session aggregations, and sliding averages over a Kafka topic are precisely the shapes a windowed SQL query expresses well — and they must run continuously, survive failures, and never silently lose an epoch of data. A Kafka-API broker such as Redpanda supplies the durable log; Arroyo turns that log into features. Batch-oriented companions like Materialize and RisingWave solve adjacent parts of the real-time SQL space, but Arroyo’s design is deliberately dataflow-first: SQL is compiled into a distributed graph, not a continuously-refreshed view.

This post walks the master branch of the repository the way the code executes: the SQL-to-DAG compiler in arroyo-planner, the serializable graph model in arroyo-datastream, the Arrow-based runtime in arroyo-worker and arroyo-operator, checkpointing in arroyo-state and arroyo-storage, and the extension layers — connectors and UDFs. Every symbol cited below was verified against the source tree, and the two diagrams were generated from the actual file structure.

Overview: SQL text flows through the DataFusion-backed planner into a logical graph, the chaining optimizer fuses stages, and the Arrow runtime executes subtasks with checkpointed state, connectors on both edges.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything is one Rust binary. The Commands, L82 enum offers run, api, controller, cluster, worker, node, and a plan Visualize subcommand.
  • The compiler entry point is parse_and_get_program, L614 — it parses SQL and plans it through DataFusion.
  • PlanToGraphVisitor, L47 walks the resulting plan and collects operators into a graph.
  • LogicalProgram, L300 is the serializable DAG; ChainingOptimizer, L18 fuses compatible neighbors to cut network hops.
  • On workers, Engine, L373 builds the physical graph and start (L528) spawns every subtask.
  • Each stage implements ArrowOperator, L1153, processing Arrow RecordBatch streams.
  • WorkerJobController, L46 drives job lifecycle and checkpoint timing.
  • TableManager, L37 snapshots keyed state per epoch into parquet files written through the StorageProvider (L56) on S3, R2, GCS, Azure, or local disk.
  • On the edges, KafkaConnector, L71 moves bytes, while UdfDylib, L168 loads user functions into running tasks.

Detail: the operator library, checkpoint mechanics, connector construction, and UDF loading, each anchored to verified files and line numbers.

In the detail view, the upper band is the compilation funnel, the middle band is the operator library that DataFusion-generated stages resolve into, and the lower bands carry durability and IO. Edges are labeled with the mechanism each hop uses — control messages, barrier propagation, batch delivery — and every box points at the exact file and line in the repository, so the diagram doubles as a reading list.

SQL In, Dataflow Out: the Compiler Path

Arroyo accepts SQL as text, either from the CLI or the API server. parse_sql, L880 tokenizes it with sqlparser through a custom ArroyoDialect. The statements are then executed against an ArroyoSchemaProvider, L118 that exposes tables backed by connectors plus the built-in function registry assembled by register_functions (L135).

User-defined functions join the session in two flavors: add_rust_udf (L329) accepts Rust source, and add_python_udf (L412) accepts Python — both are parsed at compile time so the engine knows each function’s signature before a single event flows.

DataFusion plans the query, and that is where the streaming translation happens. PlanToGraphVisitor visits each plan node — including Arroyo’s own extensions for sinks, windows, key calculation, and updating aggregates — and emits LogicalNode, L220 vertices wired by LogicalEdge, L136 edges into a petgraph DAG. The final LogicalProgram is binary-serializable, which is what lets a controller ship the compiled job to remote workers unchanged. Before handoff, ChainingOptimizer rewrites the graph (its Optimizer impl at L40) to fuse chainable stages, so a filter followed by a projection runs in one task with zero serialization between them. For library embedding rather than SQL text, parse_and_get_arrow_program (L884) exposes the same machinery programmatically.

The Runtime: Arrow Batches, Not Rows

Workers never see SQL. Engine, L373 receives the logical graph, and Program::from_logical (L210) expands every node into one subtask per parallelism slot — restoring checkpoint metadata first if the job is recovering from a stored epoch. construct_operator (L903) then instantiates each stage from a registry of constructors.

Two traits define the programming model. SourceOperator, L329 owns the head of the graph: it collects records, broadcasts watermarks, and stamps barriers. ArrowOperator, L1153 is the workhorse: on_start, process_batch, handle_watermark, and handle_checkpoint callbacks over columnar batches. Subtasks exchange batches over the network via Quad addressing (network_manager.rs, L272).

The window implementations show how much care went into Arrow-native design: TumblingAggregatingWindowFunc, L50 and SlidingAggregatingWindowFunc, L46 aggregate in fixed and overlapping panes, IncrementalAggregatingFunc, L201 maintains updating results without recomputing, and LookupJoin, L37 enriches streams from dimension tables. Event-time correctness comes from WatermarkGenerator, L35, which advances watermarks batch by batch. Pure row expressions are pushed straight into DataFusion physical plans via StatelessPhysicalExecutor (L287 in arrow/mod.rs).

Checkpoints: Parquet State and Two-Phase Commits

Fault tolerance is the most instructive part of the codebase. The WorkerJobController periodically calls its checkpoint method (L774), which starts a new epoch. A CheckpointBarrier, L492 — the epoch marker — then sweeps through the graph.

When a barrier reaches a subtask, run_checkpoint (operator.rs, L308) asks TableManager to snapshot all keyed tables via its checkpoint method (L368) and reports a FinishedSync event upstream. CheckpointState, L26 accumulates those acks (checkpoint_event, L217), assembles CheckpointMetadata (build_metadata, L416), and — once every subtask has reported — flips into CommittingState, L6 through into_commit (L475). The controller’s send_commit_messages (L794) then commits: a two-phase protocol so sinks publish only after the whole graph agrees the epoch is durable.

The state itself is ordinary parquet. StateBackend is a type alias for ParquetBackend, L25 (see the alias at state/lib.rs, L54), and files land on StorageProvider — S3, R2, GCS, Azure, or local paths (config structs at L199-L228). Because checkpoint files are just parquet, they are inspectable and debuggable with ordinary tooling, a small but real operational win.

Connectors and UDFs: the Extension Points

The IO layer separates configuration from execution. Connection, L23 models a profile plus table config, and every connector implements the Connector, L68 trait; a connectors registry (L39 in arroyo-connectors/src/lib.rs) exposes them by name. The repository ships Kafka, Kinesis, NATS, MQTT, Fluvio, Redis, WebSocket, Webhook, HTTP polling, impulse, and filesystem connectors — the latter writing parquet, JSON, Delta, or Iceberg tables.

Kafka is the canonical example. KafkaConnector, L71 implements Connector (L170) with a from_config factory (L199). Its source half, KafkaSourceFunc, L32, implements SourceOperator (L298); get_consumer (L55) builds the rdkafka consumer, and consumer offsets are persisted as KafkaState (L49) with each checkpoint epoch, so recovery resumes exactly where the last commit left off.

UDFs follow a compile-and-load pattern. The #[udf] proc macro (udf-macros, L62) generates wrappers and type metadata; ParsedUdfFile, L53 parses the submitted Rust source; UdfDylib, L168 loads the compiled library into the task, with an async variant AsyncUdfDylib (L257) for IO-bound functions. Python functions run through PythonUDF, L29 in an embedded interpreter with pyarrow exchange.

From Install to Your First Model

Arroyo ships as a single binary. On macOS use brew install arroyosystems/tap/arroyo, on macOS or Linux run curl -LsSf https://arroyo.dev/install.sh | sh, or start it in Docker with docker run -p 5115:5115 ghcr.io/arroyosystems/arroyo:latest. Launch arroyo cluster and open the web UI at http://localhost:5115; for one local job without the cluster, arroyo run takes a query file directly (RunArgs at L59, executed by run, L400).

Your first “model” does not need a GPU — it needs features. The repository’s own analytics_tutorial.sql test fixture shows the query shape over a Kafka topic; adapted, it computes one-minute rolling hit counts per URL, exactly the kind of input a ranking model consumes:

CREATE TABLE events (
    time TIMESTAMP,
    path TEXT
) WITH (
    connector = 'kafka',
    format = 'json',
    type = 'source',
    bootstrap_servers = 'localhost:9092',
    topic = 'events'
);

CREATE TABLE features (
    time TIMESTAMP,
    path TEXT,
    hits BIGINT
) WITH (
    connector = 'kafka',
    format = 'json',
    type = 'sink',
    bootstrap_servers = 'localhost:9092',
    topic = 'features'
);

INSERT INTO features
SELECT window.end, path, count
FROM (
    SELECT count(*) AS count, path,
           hop(interval '5 seconds', '1 minute') AS window
    FROM events
    GROUP BY path, window
);

hop(interval '5 seconds', '1 minute') is Arroyo’s sliding-window sugar — a one-minute window advanced every five seconds. Produce a few JSON events to the events topic and the features topic starts receiving per-minute counts continuously, checkpointed against failure.

Honest Limits

No source tour can prove what the code does not show, so the claims below are restricted to what the README states and what the checked-out tree reveals:

  • Performance: the README claims scaling “up to millions of events per second”; that is a project claim, and we ran no benchmarks for this tour.
  • Control plane: the API and controller expect Postgres or SQLite (DatabaseType dispatch in main.rs at L311); the single-binary cluster command embeds API, compiler, and controller together (start_control_plane, L445).
  • WASM: the graph model still defines WasmUDF types (datastream lib.rs, L49), but the UDF host we traced on master loads dynamic libraries and Python; we did not find a WASM executor wired into the runtime crates we read, so treat WASM UDFs as legacy surface, not a current feature path.
  • Exactly-once semantics: the two-phase commit machinery is real, but end-to-end guarantees depend on each sink’s connector implementation; the filesystem sink, for instance, carries its own two-phase committer.
  • Scheduling: the controller includes a Kubernetes scheduler (crates/arroyo-controller/src/schedulers/kubernetes/), but we only read code — no cluster deployments were exercised here.
  • This article is a source tour of one snapshot of master; APIs move fast, so anchor to the line links rather than quoting behavior from memory.
entry.summary: A guided tour through the Arroyo source tree: how Rust, DataFusion and Arrow turn SQL over Kafka topics into a checkpointed distributed dataflow.

entry.title: Bytewax Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Python Stream Processing on a Rust Timely Core

link.title: Bytewax Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Python Stream Processing on a Rust Timely Core

entry.content:
Every serious ML system eventually hits the same wall: the features that feed your model have to be computed continuously, on live data, with state that survives crashes. Batch scoring is not enough once tokens, clicks, sensor readings, or order events arrive per second. Bytewax attacks exactly this gap — it is a Python-native stream processing framework whose execution engine is written in Rust on top of Timely Dataflow. You express a dataflow with ordinary Python functions and operators, and a compiled extension distributes that computation across workers and processes.

What makes Bytewax interesting as a codebase, compared with the engines we have toured before such as Arroyo and RisingWave, is that the Python API is not a thin shell over an embedded SQL planner. Instead, the Dataflow object you build in Python is a declarative record of steps, and Rust code walks that record and reconstructs the whole thing as Timely operators. The language boundary is a compiler boundary: Python describes, Rust executes. That split — plus an SQLite-backed recovery journal and a confluent-kafka connector — is what we traced in the source.

We cloned bytewax/bytewax at branch main and read three areas: pysrc/bytewax (the Python package), src (the Rust crate), and examples. The two diagrams below were generated from the actual file tree, and every symbol cited in this post was verified against the checkout — line numbers anchor claims so you can jump straight from this page into the source.

Overview: the Python operator API and connectors on the left, the CLI entry points in the middle, and the Rust Timely core plus recovery journal on the right.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • wordcount.py, L17 is the smallest complete dataflow: op.input, op.map, op.flat_map, op.count_final, op.output — five calls, one running program.
  • Dataflow, L178 is a dataclass that records the operator tree, and Stream, L214 is the typed handle that links one step’s output to the next step’s input.
  • map, L2499 sits in the operator library; each public operator is a decorated function that appends a step to the flow and returns a new Stream.
  • window, L1256 adds event-time windows on top, driven by an EventClock, L361 with watermarks and a TumblingWindower, L897 (sliding and session windowers share the same interface).
  • FixedPartitionedSource, L144 is the source contract for partitioned inputs; KafkaSource, L340 implements it over confluent-kafka.
  • run.py, L343 is what executes when you type python -m bytewax.run: argparse parses workers, addresses, and recovery flags, imports your flow, then hands everything to Rust cli_main.
  • run_main, L114 and cluster_main, L239 are the Rust entry points, registered into the _bytewax PyO3 module at mod_bytewax, L26.
  • build_production_dataflow, L255 is the heart of execution: it walks the Python step tree and constructs real Timely operators.
  • write_recovery, L1707 persists state snapshots into the journal, and load_snaps, L1638 replays them on restart.

Detail: from the Python `Dataflow` model through the operator API and Kafka connector, across the PyO3 bridge into the Timely worker, dispatch, and the SQLite recovery journal.

The Operator API: Where Python Meets the Core

The public surface lives in pysrc/bytewax. Stateless operators such as map, filter, and flat_map wrap a Python callable and are almost self-explanatory. The stateful half is more instructive. stateful, L1067 takes a builder and asks you to implement the StatefulLogic, L919 abstract class: on_item processes one item per key, on_notify fires timers, and snapshot returns picklable state. That last method is not decoration — it is the exact hook the recovery journal uses. Internally, every stateful operator, including join at join, L2326 and the windowing operator, compiles down to a single core primitive: stateful_batch, L797, wrapped by the StatefulBatchLogic, L594 adapter. One primitive, snapshotted one way, powers the whole stateful surface.

The @operator decorator itself does more than registration: it type-checks ports, generates stable step IDs, and lets operators compose. Composite operators are real: op.collect at collect, L1150 and fold_final at fold_final, L1946 are written against StatefulLogic, the same primitives you would use, so reading the library source doubles as a tutorial for writing your own operators. Keyed streams are the state boundary — key_on, L2377 converts any stream into a KeyedStream, and every stateful operator requires one, which is why per-key routing is visible in the execution core rather than hidden as an implementation detail. For read-mostly enrichment, enrich_cached, L1316 pairs a TTL cache with a lookup function so reference data does not have to flow through the stream.

Inside the Timely Execution Core

The src directory is a Rust crate compiled as a PyO3 extension module named _bytewax. When run_main receives your flow, it extracts the Python Dataflow into a Rust wrapper (dataflow.rs, L8) and starts a Timely computation. Worker, L40 then drives the event loop until the probe reports done — epochs advance on a configurable interval, which is how time is coordinated across workers.

The translation step is build_production_dataflow, L255. It pushes steps onto a stack and dispatches on core operator names: input, inspect_debug, merge, output, redistribute, and stateful_batch (the arm is at worker.rs, L447). For input, it checks whether the Python source object is a fixed-partitioned or dynamic source and calls the matching builder; for stateful_batch, it hands control to the Rust-side Timely operator at operators.rs, L445, which batches items per epoch, calls into your Python logic, and drains snapshot bytes for recovery. One subtlety visible in the builder is that composite Python operators never reach this dispatch directly: when the step on the stack is not a core operator, the builder pops its substeps at worker.rs, L468 and pushes them back for expansion, so by the time the stack unwinds, every node in the Timely graph is one of a handful of primitives. Multi-process runs go through cluster_main, L239, with worker counts parsed into WorkerCount, L309. If you want the visual version of your own flow, to_mermaid, L302 renders the step graph as Mermaid.

Recovery: an SQLite Journal of Epochs

Bytewax’s fault tolerance is epoch-based. Every stateful operator emits a snapshot each epoch; those snapshot streams are concatenated and fed to write_recovery, L1707, which writes them through per-partition writers into SQLite databases configured by RecoveryConfig, L319. The schema is managed with SQLite migrations, and each part also records execution metadata and frontier information so a restarted cluster can agree on where to resume. On restart, load_snaps, L1638 streams the snapshots back before the resume epoch, and build_production_dataflow wires them into each operator’s initial state — so a crash costs you at most the last epoch interval, not the whole run. Writing is batched through a RecoveryCommitter, L943 that flushes committed epoch data, and a test named gc_leaves_only_final_snap at recovery.rs, L992 documents the retention rule the journal applies when pruning. The Python side stays thin: passing -r <dir> plus -s and -b intervals makes run.py, L343 construct the config that crosses the bridge.

Kafka In, Insights Out

The connector package wraps confluent-kafka, the Python client over librdkafka. KafkaSource, L340 manages one consumer per partition, resumes from committed offsets, and emits KafkaSourceMessage, L92 records that carry key, value, offset, and timestamp. The ergonomic layer is the operator pair at kafka.input, L91 and output, which build the source and KafkaSink, L537 in one call. Deserialization is its own layer: the operators deserialize_key, deserialize_value, and deserialize, L273 turn raw bytes into JSON or Python objects on the stream, with serialize and friends at serialize, L396 on the way out, so byte handling never leaks into your business logic. Since the connector is just an implementation of the source ABCs, swapping brokers is a config change — our Kafka and Redpanda source tours cover the server side of that pairing.

From Install to Your First Model

Start with pip install bytewax. Save the wordcount example as wordcount.py, then run it with python -m bytewax.run wordcount.py; add -w 2 to run two workers in one process, or pass --addresses and --process-id to form a cluster across machines. For serving an ML model on a stream, the pattern from the source is direct: op.input from KafkaSource, op.map to deserialize and call your model (an ONNX or scikit-learn scorer inside a plain Python function), op.key_on followed by op.stateful to maintain per-user features, then op.output back to Kafka. waxctl df deploy packages the same flow file for Kubernetes deployments, and the repository’s own examples directory covers joins, windowing, and Redpanda serdes beyond wordcount. To inspect what you built, python -m bytewax.visualize prints the flow as Mermaid text you can paste into a README.

Honest Limits

Everything above was verified by reading the repository at main on 2026-11-04; we ran no benchmarks and claim none. A few practical caveats surface in the source itself. First, recovery is opt-in and requires all three flags — -r, -s, and -b — otherwise the CLI refuses to start, so out of the box your dataflow state is ephemeral. Second, KafkaSink extends DynamicSink, the stateless sink contract, and the recovery machinery in src/recovery.rs tracks stateful operators — the journal protects your aggregation state, while output delivery semantics depend on the sink implementation. Third, the Rust internals are pub(crate): the Python API is the only supported contract, so operator behavior can shift between releases; the changelog and migration guide are worth reading before upgrading. Finally, Bytewax is a dataflow engine, not a SQL database — if you want streaming SQL instead of Python operators, our earlier tours of Arroyo and RisingWave cover that style of engine.
entry.summary: A source tour of bytewax/bytewax showing how the Python operator API compiles down to Timely Dataflow operators in Rust, with an SQLite recovery journal and confluent-kafka connectors.

entry.title: Inside Materialize: A Source Tour of the Rust Streaming Database That Compiles SQL into Dataflows

link.title: Inside Materialize: A Source Tour of the Rust Streaming Database That Compiles SQL into Dataflows

entry.content:
If you have ever wired an ML feature store, you know the pain: features are computed offline, batched into a table, and served stale by the time your model reads them. Materialize attacks that problem from an unusual direction — it is a PostgreSQL-compatible database that keeps your SQL views continuously, transactionally up to date as the underlying data changes. Its own README pitches exactly the use case this blog cares about: delivering fresh context for AI and RAG applications, operational dashboards, and real-time products, without hand-rolling custom streaming plumbing. The payoff is one system acting as a cache, a streaming job, and a warehouse at the same time.

What makes Materialize special is not “another streaming engine”. RisingWave, which we toured earlier this week, walks a similar road; Redpanda gives you the event log underneath; but Materialize’s pitch is correctness: every query answer is the correct result on some specific, recent version of your data, even for joins across multiple upstream systems, and never an approximate or eventually consistent one. Under the hood it recasts your SQL as dataflows — incremental, reactive computation graphs built on the timely and differential dataflow libraries, the same research lineage that powers Materialize’s niche in the streaming space.

This post is a source tour of MaterializeInc/materialize (Rust, branch main). We will walk four crates that together form the whole machine: adapter (the coordinator that speaks SQL), storage (ingestion from Kafka and Postgres CDC), compute (timely/differential workers that maintain views), and persist (durable storage). Two diagrams anchor the tour — an overview first, then a detail view with the actual files and entry points.

Overview: the coordinator (adapter crate) drives storage and compute clusters; both layers land their data in the persist layer, which reduces to Blob and Consensus abstractions.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The Coordinator, L1908 is the heart of the SQL layer. It bootstraps the environment, owns the catalog, and multiplexes every client command through one message loop — the same process that serves the PostgreSQL wire protocol.
  • DDL does not execute imperatively. Statements are sequenced: sequence_create_source, L634 shows the staged pattern, where each plan step is deterministic and resumable.
  • Provisioning is centralized in the cluster controller. ClusterControllerRequest, L66 models the request vocabulary for starting, resizing, and routing to storage and compute replicas.
  • On the ingestion side, serve, L56 is the entry point of the storaged process, which renders every source and sink assigned to a storage cluster.
  • Source-native progress is normalized by ReclockOperator, L36, which maps Kafka offsets and Postgres LSNs onto Materialize’s timestamp timeline.
  • For queries, serve, L184 boots the timely worker set of a compute replica, and ComputeState, L177 is the per-worker registry of dataflows, arrangements, peeks, and subscriptions.
  • Everything durable bottoms out in two abstractions: Blob, L566 for immutable, versioned buffers, and Consensus, L442 for a linearizable compare-and-swap log.

Detail: per-crate call graph with verified file paths — from statement sequencing and timestamp selection down to Avro decoding, RocksDB upsert state, parquet-encoded trace batches, and hedged blob reads.

The Coordinator: Where SQL Meets Streaming

The adapter crate is the brain. When a client connects, it looks exactly like a Postgres server on the wire, but CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW does something no ordinary database does: it registers a long-lived dataflow instead of snapshotting a result. The coordinator’s bootstrap, L2395 replays the catalog on startup, then hands each incoming statement to the sequencer. For materialized views specifically, create_materialized_view_finish, L563 optimizes the query, installs the dataflow in a compute cluster, and commits the definition to the catalog — in that order, atomically.

Query time is the subtle part. A SELECT must answer at a single logical timestamp where all its inputs are readable. TimestampDetermination, L761 is the structure that pins a query to such an as-of time, and PeekClient, L64 then races the peek out to replicas. If one replica is slow or fails, another answers — multi-active replication falls out of the design rather than being bolted on.

Ingestion: Kafka and Postgres CDC in storaged

The storage crate turns external systems into timestamped collections. The shape of each source is the same three-stage composition: read raw updates, decode them into typed rows, then reclock source-native progress into Materialize timestamps. Kafka topics arrive as partition readers — KafkaSourceReader, L110 — with an Avro path in AvroDecoderState, L16 that understands Confluent schema-registry payloads. For upsert semantics, keyed state is spilled to RocksDB, L22, so a backfill of a huge topic does not have to fit in RAM.

The CDC sources are the ones your AI feature work will likely use. ensure_replication_slot, L442 takes a consistent snapshot of your tables and then tails Postgres’ logical replication stream, using the LSN as native progress. MySQL replication follows the same pattern in src/storage/src/source/mysql/. All of this per-worker wiring is coordinated by StorageState, L300, which also drives the async storage worker that publishes progress. If you run Redpanda or Kafka in your stack, this is the code that consumes them; we benchmarked those brokers separately on this blog.

Compute: Timely Workers, Arrangements, Differential Joins

The compute crate is where differential dataflow earns its keep. The core idea is compact enough for a paragraph: every collection is a set of (data, time, diff) triples, and every operator — join, reduce, top-k — is written once against that abstraction so it can recompute only what changed, when logical time advances along a partial order. That is why Materialize can maintain a multi-way join over live CDC streams without recomputing the world on every update, and why queries have coherent answers instead of tearing across partial updates. build_compute_dataflow, L210 lowers an optimized plan into operators, with render_plan, L1161 dispatching each operator kind — joins, reduces, top-k — to its implementation. The resulting arrangements (indexed, incrementally maintainable multisets) are kept alive and compacted by TraceManager, L33.

Reads and outputs flow through the same state machine. One-shot SELECTs run via serve_index_peek, L1193, which waits until the arrangement’s frontier passes the query’s as-of time. Continuous outputs use sinks: persist_sink, L240 streams a materialized view’s output into durable shards, and subscribe, L83 implements the SUBSCRIBE tail protocol. Memory pressure is not an afterthought — start_limiter, L41 reserves global budgets so a replica degrades predictably instead of getting OOM-killed mid-query.

Persist: Blob and Consensus

Durability is deliberately two-trait simple. Blob, L566 stores immutable buffers; Consensus, L442 provides a linearizable CAS over a short log that records each shard’s current state and upper frontier. Implementations swap by URL scheme: FileBlob, L45 for single-node local runs (CRC-checked), Postgres/CRDB-backed consensus and S3/GCS/Azure blobs for cloud deployments — MinIO works fine as the S3 endpoint for experiments.

Two production details are worth stealing for your own systems. First, tail latency: HedgedBlob, L236 fires a second read when the first is slow, hiding object-storage hiccups. Second, columnar efficiency: encode_trace_parquet, L43 packs trace batches into parquet before they land in blobs, which is what makes “near-infinite storage” in the README more than marketing.

From Install to Your First Model

Here is the fastest loop, all of it straight from the repository’s README. Grab the community edition from materialize.com/download (free forever under 24 GiB of memory and 48 GiB of disk), run materialized or the Docker image, and point psql at it — it speaks the PostgreSQL protocol, so any driver works. Then create a demo source and a materialized view:

CREATE SOURCE tpch
  FROM LOAD GENERATOR TPCH (SCALE FACTOR 1)
  FOR ALL TABLES;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW tpch_q15 AS
  SELECT s_suppkey, s_name, s_address, s_phone, total_revenue
  FROM supplier, revenue
  WHERE s_suppkey = supplier_no
    AND total_revenue = (SELECT max(total_revenue) FROM revenue);

CREATE INDEX tpch_q15_idx ON tpch_q15 (s_suppkey);

The load generator streams inserts, updates, and deletes on the underlying tables, and Materialize keeps tpch_q15 incrementally updated the whole time. SELECT * FROM tpch_q15 returns current results immediately — no REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, no cache invalidation, no cron. Getting data out is symmetric: the README documents both pull-based access through any PostgreSQL-compatible driver and push-based tails — SUBSCRIBE streams every change to a view as it lands, and sinks can forward the same updates to a Kafka topic or copy them to object storage.

For an ML serving stack, the pattern maps directly: define your features as views over CDC sources, let the coordinator and compute workers maintain them continuously, and have your Python inference service query them like an ordinary Postgres database — or tail them with SUBSCRIBE for streaming inference.

Honest Limits

Everything above comes from the README and the source; none of it is a benchmark, and we ran none. Limits worth knowing before you build: the community edition’s free tier is bounded by those 24/48 GiB figures — real production scale historically means the managed cloud or an enterprise deployment. The SQL dialect is a large but not complete subset of PostgreSQL; check the docs for the functions you rely on. Persist’s Consensus currently targets Postgres/CockroachDB and blobs target the big three object stores, so fully air-gapped, single-binary deployments trade you back into local file durability. And while the load generators are excellent for demos, your own Postgres CDC source will need a replication slot — plan the primary’s disk and wal_keep settings accordingly, or the source will misbehave at snapshot time. Finally, this tour reflects branch main at a point in time; the codebase moves fast, and file paths will drift. Materialize maintains views; it does not replace a broker — you still want Kafka or Redpanda upstream and a serving layer downstream, and Materialize is the correctness-preserving middle that makes both smarter.
entry.summary: A guided tour of the Materialize Rust source, from the SQL coordinator and timely dataflow workers to Postgres CDC sources and durable persist shards.

entry.title: Inside Apache Pulsar: The Stateless Broker, BookKeeper Ledgers, and the Managed-Ledger Stitch

link.title: Inside Apache Pulsar: The Stateless Broker, BookKeeper Ledgers, and the Managed-Ledger Stitch

entry.content:
Modern ML systems are, underneath everything else, nervous systems. Feature vectors flow from ingestion jobs to training clusters, prediction requests emit traces, drift monitors and shadow scorers consume the same tensors in parallel, and retraining jobs wake up when enough new data has accumulated. All of that is event transport, and event transport at multi-team scale is where Apache Pulsar makes a distinctive bet. Unlike a single-log design such as Redpanda or the classic Kafka architecture we toured in Kafka, Pulsar splits the job in two: a fleet of stateless brokers that serve traffic, and BookKeeper bookies that actually hold the bytes. That separation is why Pulsar is popular for ML event buses where tenancy, fan-out patterns, and storage elasticity vary wildly between teams — one tenant streams embeddings at high fan-out, another archives inference logs for months, and neither should need to rebalance disks when the other grows.

The second Pulsar-specific draw for AI infrastructure is multi-tenancy as a first-class concept. A namespace carries its own retention, replication, and BookKeeper durability policy, so a training-data topic and a health-metrics topic can live on the same cluster with wildly different guarantees. And because the storage layer is decoupled, a cold backlog — say, six months of prompts retained for audit — does not occupy the serving hot path. RisingWave and similar stream processors can then consume from Pulsar the same way they consume from Kafka, treating the broker as the durable front door.

This post is a source tour of how that works, read directly from the Java on master of apache/pulsar. We walk four modules: pulsar-broker (the serving layer), pulsar-common and pulsar-client-admin-api (naming and policies), and managed-ledger (the storage abstraction over BookKeeper). Two diagrams anchor the tour — a compact overview and a deeper detail map — and every symbol we cite is linked to its real location in the repository.

Overview: from process entry to BookKeeper-backed storage — the broker serving layer in the middle, naming and policies on one side, the managed ledger on the other.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • A broker process boots through PulsarService.start, L910, which wires the metadata store and constructs the broker’s serving components.
  • BrokerService.getTopic, L1432 is the topic registry: it resolves an incoming topic name to a Topic object, creating one if the client is allowed to auto-create.
  • Before a topic can load, NamespaceService.getBundleAsync, L282 finds the NamespaceBundle, L27 that contains it — the hash-range unit one broker claims exclusively.
  • TopicName.get, L80 parses the persistent://tenant/namespace/topic URI, and getPartitionIndex, L361 maps partitioned topics onto plain non-partitioned subtopics.
  • On the write path, PersistentTopic.publishMessage, L684 hands the payload to the managed ledger, and addComplete, L804 runs when the entry is durably stored.
  • PersistencePolicies, L29 carries the durability knobs — bookkeeperEnsemble, bookkeeperWriteQuorum, and bookkeeperAckQuorum at lines 30–32 — that decide how many bookies store each entry.
  • The storage itself lives in ManagedLedgerImpl.asyncAddEntry, L989, whose per-append work is embodied by OpAddEntry.run, L254.
  • On the read side, PersistentSubscription.acknowledgeMessageAsync, L499 advances the subscription cursor through ManagedCursorImpl.markDelete, L2219.
  • Finally, readMoreEntries, L54 decides how eagerly the broker fetches entries for consumers, which is where backpressure actually happens.

Detail: the publish path through deduplication into the ledger engine, the three dispatcher families, cursor persistence, and the tiered-storage offloader hook.

The Broker Layer: A Registry, Not a Storage Engine

The most important thing to internalize about BrokerService is that it stores nothing. Its class declaration, L236 opens a component that is essentially a concurrent map from topic names to Topic instances plus the machinery to load and unload them. When a producer connects, PersistentTopic.addProducer, L910 validates and registers it; the topic itself implements the ledger callback interface — see the class line, L223 — so the managed ledger calls back into it when an append lands.

That design has a concrete payoff for ML fleets: broker restarts and rollouts do not move data, only ownership. The topic’s getSubscriptions, L2973 map is rebuilt from the metadata store when a new broker takes over. Optional quality gates hang off the same class: MessageDeduplication, L55 lets producer retries stay idempotent (useful when a flaky edge job re-sends feature batches), and checkMessageExpiry, L2577 enforces TTLs so stale telemetry does not accumulate forever. Geo-replication is likewise just another reader of the local ledger — GeoPersistentReplicator republishes entries to remote clusters, which is how teams keep training-event streams in sync across regions.

Ledgers, Cursors, and the Managed-Ledger Stitch

The managed-ledger module is where Pulsar quietly reinvents a segmented log on top of BookKeeper. A managed ledger is, at heart, an ordered list of BookKeeper ledgers plus a set of cursors. ManagedLedgerImpl, L165 opens with the ledger list in hand; MetaStoreImpl.getManagedLedgerInfo, L105 is where that list and the cursor metadata are read and written. When the current ledger fills up, rollCurrentLedgerIfFull, L2486 seals it and opens a fresh one, so individual ledgers stay bounded no matter how long the topic lives.

Cursors are the other half of the story. Every subscription owns a cursor, created through asyncOpenCursor, L1216, and a cursor is just a durable position: ManagedCursorImpl, L124 persists ack state through internalMarkDelete, L2718. Because each consumer’s position is independent, one slow drift-detection job can lag months behind a hot scorer without blocking anyone. Once all cursors have moved past a ledger, trimConsumedLedgersInBackground, L3597 schedules deletion via internalTrimConsumedLedgers, L3811 — retention is implemented as “nobody needs these ledgers anymore,” which is a cleaner model than per-partition log compaction. In practice a topic’s footprint is a function of its live cursors rather than of any static disk assignment: the write head rolls forward relentlessly, and each ledger dies quietly once the last consumer has crossed it.

Tiered storage plugs in at exactly this seam. LedgerOffloader, L37 defines the SPI, and its offload, L137 method moves a sealed ledger to object storage while the ledger’s metadata keeps pointing at the offload copy. For ML audit trails that must be retained far longer than they are read, this is the difference between an affordable cluster and an unaffordable one.

Dispatch: Three Subscriptions, One Read Path

Pulsar’s subscription types are famous in its docs, but in the source they are three dispatcher classes behind one interface. PersistentSubscription, L99 attaches the right one per subscription. Exclusive and failover modes use PersistentDispatcherSingleActiveConsumer, L63; shared mode uses PersistentDispatcherMultipleConsumers, L87; and key-shared mode uses PersistentStickyKeyDispatcherMultipleConsumers, L67, which hashes message keys onto consumers so per-key ordering survives parallel consumption. All of them obey the same read-throttling loop, and DispatchRateLimiter, L32 caps how fast each topic can push messages downstream.

For ML teams the choice is meaningful in practice: exclusive suits a single trainer that must see events exactly in order; shared suits stateless scorers that only care about throughput; key-shared suits enrichment services that need per-entity ordering without dedicating a whole consumer group. The important source-level insight is that these are dispatch policies over the same ledger — the storage format never changes.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest way to feel the architecture is to run it locally, where Pulsar collapses broker, bookie, and metadata store into one process. The repository README documents the entry point: bin/pulsar standalone starts a standalone service, and conf/standalone.conf holds the merged broker-plus-bookie configuration. Assuming you have a JDK 17+ and the binary distribution unpacked:

bin/pulsar standalone

Then, in a second terminal, produce and consume on a topic — this exercises the exact path we read above, from TopicName parsing to a managed ledger with one ledger and one cursor:

bin/pulsar-client produce ml-events --messages '{"model":"churn-v3","split":"train","rows":512}'
bin/pulsar-client consume ml-events -s trainer-sub -n 1

From Python, the official client mirrors the same concepts. Install it with pip install pulsar-client, then publish training events and consume them with a shared subscription, which matches the dispatcher class we read:

import pulsar, json

client = pulsar.Client("pulsar://localhost:6650")
producer = client.create_producer("persistent://public/default/ml-events")
producer.send(json.dumps({
    "event": "training_batch",
    "model": "churn-v3",
    "rows": 512,
    "ts": "2026-11-04T09:30:00Z",
}).encode())

reader = client.subscribe("persistent://public/default/ml-events",
                          subscription_name="drift-monitor",
                          consumer_type=pulsar.ConsumerType.Shared)
msg = reader.receive()
print("got:", msg.data().decode())
reader.acknowledge(msg)
client.close()

A training loop can publish one event per batch, and a drift monitor can attach its own subscription and replay from the earliest retained message — two independent cursors over one ledger, exactly as the source shows. Once the service is up, the sibling scripts bin/pulsar-admin and bin/pulsar-shell, shipped in the same directory of the repository, let you create namespaces and inspect bundles, which is a convenient way to watch ownership move between brokers in a multi-node setup.

Namespaces, Bundles, and Cheap Multi-Tenancy

The last piece is the tenancy model. A namespace is sliced into bundles — NamespaceBundle, L27 is that unit — and each bundle is served by exactly one broker at a time, with ownership recorded in the metadata store. Spreading a busy namespace across brokers is a metadata operation, not a data copy. Durability, meanwhile, is declared per namespace through PersistencePolicies, L29: the ensemble size decides how many bookies form the write set, the write quorum how many receive each entry, and the ack quorum how many must confirm before a publish completes. A high-value inference-log namespace can demand three-way quorum writes while a low-value metrics namespace trades durability for latency, on the same bookies. If you compared this with Redpanda’s Raft-per-partition model, the contrast is stark: Pulsar moves replication out of the broker process entirely and into a shared, bookie-level storage fabric.

Honest Limits

Everything above is read from the source on master, not measured. We did not benchmark throughput or latency, and the dispatcher code is under active refactoring — the async read paths we linked are intricate, and real behavior depends on configuration we did not exercise. We deliberately skipped large subsystems: Functions and IO connectors live outside pulsar-broker, transactions are in their own module, the proxy and WebSocket layers were not toured, and the tiered-storage providers (for example the blob-store offloader under tiered-storage/) were only cited through their interface. Line numbers refer to master as of 2026-11-04 and will drift. Treat the CLI commands shown earlier as documentation-level examples rather than exhaustive references; the --help output of the release you run is the authority. If you want the contrasting designs, our Kafka tour covers the log-per-partition baseline and RisingWave shows what consumes these events downstream.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Apache Pulsar's Java broker, its managed-ledger storage engine, and the namespace policies that wire topics to BookKeeper ledgers.

entry.title: Inside Redpanda: A C++ Source Tour of the Kafka-Compatible Streaming Engine

link.title: Inside Redpanda: A C++ Source Tour of the Kafka-Compatible Streaming Engine

entry.content:
Modern ML systems live and die on event streams. Training features arrive as sequences of user actions, model predictions come back as telemetry, and drift detection watches both. The infrastructure that carries those events has traditionally been the JVM: Apache Kafka plus ZooKeeper, plus the operational weight of both. Redpanda takes a different road — it reimplements the Kafka wire protocol as a single C++ binary built on the Seastar thread-per-core framework, with no ZooKeeper and no JVM, and it embeds its own Raft implementation instead of relying on an external coordinator. If you have followed our Kafka coverage, this is the engine that speaks the same protocol while owning every layer underneath.

Why should that matter to an AI/ML practitioner? Because inference platforms are streaming systems in disguise. A feature store ingesting click events, an online scorer emitting latency traces, an agent framework appending tool calls — all of them want a durable, replayable log with Kafka’s client ecosystem. Understanding how Redpanda turns a Produce request into a quorum-replicated disk write helps you reason about the durability and ordering guarantees your training and serving data actually get. And because there is no garbage collector on the serving path, the tail-latency profile differs from a JVM broker — which matters when the same stream feeds both a nightly training job and a real-time scorer. In this tour we read the source directly — every symbol below links into the repository at the dev branch, verified with grep before citation.

We generated two architecture diagrams from the source tree. The overview shows the three macro-layers; the detail diagram zooms into 33 components across wire protocol, replication, and disk IO. Every node in the SVG links to the corresponding file on GitHub.

Redpanda overview: the Kafka API server on the left, the embedded Raft consensus layer in the middle, and the storage engine on the right. Click any node to open the source file.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • server, L55 — one Kafka server per Seastar shard accepts client connections on the shared listener; there is no broker thread pool, each core owns its sockets exclusively.
  • connection_context, L234 — per-connection state; its process() loop, L284 reads request headers, applies quota throttling, and dispatches.
  • handler_interface, L25 — every Kafka API key is a type-erased handler; handler_for_key(), L123 resolves key 0 (Produce), key 1 (Fetch), and the rest at runtime.
  • acks_to_replicate_options(), L73 — the translation point where Kafka’s acks=-1/1/0 become Raft’s quorum_ack, leader_ack, and no_ack consistency levels.
  • partition_append(), L136 — adapts the incoming Kafka batch and calls partition.replicate() on the Raft layer; the response future completes only once the chosen consistency level is satisfied.
  • consensus, L69 — one Raft instance per partition, owning elections, replication, and the linearizable_barrier(), L221 used for read-your-writes semantics.
  • log_manager, L167 — the sharded factory whose manage(), L176 opens or creates the on-disk log for an ntp (namespace/topic/partition).
  • disk_log_impl, L48 — the Kafka-style log: an ordered segment set with appends, reads, time queries, and retention.
  • storage::api, L29 — the sharded storage entry point bundling the log manager and key/value store that every Raft group appends through.

The detailed view: 33 components from the Kafka wire protocol through Raft replication mechanics down to segment appenders, batch caching, and compaction.

How a Produce Request Becomes a Quorum Entry

The produce path is the spine of the whole system. A client sends a Kafka-encoded batch; the server decodes it into a request_context, L88 and hands it to the produce handler. Two details are worth pausing on. First, Redpanda does not convert your batch: the produce handler reuses the Kafka record batch wire format as its native log format, so a produce request is essentially what lands on disk. Second, the acks mapping in acks_to_replicate_options() is where client-facing semantics meet consensus theory — acks=-1 demands a majority of replicas to persist the entry, while acks=0 fires and forgets.

The produce handler also runs dedicated validation (produce_validation.cc) before anything is replicated, and error mapping translates Raft-level failures (not leader, truncated entry) back into the Kafka error codes clients expect. The dual scheduling-group design shows up in scheduling_group_override(), L92: produce and fetch requests run in separate Seastar scheduling groups so a burst of one cannot starve the other.

Discoverability and admission control are handled just as explicitly. Clients negotiate with ApiVersions first, and the handler table answers with the supported ranges (see serialize_apis, L40). Backpressure starts before decoding even completes — memory_estimate(), L63 reserves semaphore units per request so one oversized batch cannot push the broker toward out-of-memory, and per-client bandwidth caps live in quota_manager, L57.

The Raft Layer: Elections, Heartbeats, Batching

Redpanda implements Raft from scratch rather than embedding a library. vote_stm, L39 drives elections when a leader dies; heartbeat_manager, L87 batches per-group heartbeats so a node hosting hundreds of partitions does not send hundreds of separate RPCs. This is the same consensus algorithm that powers etcd, but wired directly into the storage engine instead of running beside it.

The write path is where the engineering shows. replicate_batcher, L26 coalesces concurrent replicate() calls from many produce requests into a single append-entries round — amortizing network and disk costs across all the producers hitting a partition. Each follower interaction gets its own replicate_entries_stm, L70, while the follower side serializes concurrent appends through append_entries_buffer, L126. follower_states, L158 tracks the match index per replica, and when a follower falls too far behind, recovery_stm, L26 streams the backlog from segments rather than the log tail.

Above Raft sit replicated state machines built on persisted_stm_base, L168 — and Redpanda practices what it preaches: Kafka consumer groups are themselves a replicated state machine, managed by group_manager, L123 and routed by shard through the group router. Even group offsets are Raft log entries. Leadership itself is carefully guarded: is_leader(), L200 gates every append, and step_down(), L365 lets a broker shed leadership cleanly during restarts, rebalances, or manual transfers.

The Storage Layer: Segments, Appenders, Compaction

The storage engine reads like a textbook Kafka log, implemented in modern C++. log_manager, L167 hands out disk_log_impl, L48 instances; each log owns a segment_set, L39 of immutable segments plus one active segment. Writes flow through segment_appender, L47, whose append(record_batch), L130 performs buffered, alignment-friendly sequential writes with fsync delegated to the background — the classic pattern for spinning-disk-friendly throughput that also happens to like NVMe.

Reads are just as carefully layered: disk_log_impl make_reader, L126 serves fetch requests, a batch_cache, L102 keeps recently written batches in memory for hot consumers, and readers_cache reuses open segment readers across concurrent fetches. The fetch machinery itself runs requests through a dedicated fetch_worker, L659 whose planners — like simple_fetch_planner, L1306 — decide how far ahead of the consumer to read, while fetch_session_cache, L35 powers incremental fetch sessions so unchanged partitions are not re-advertised on every poll. Because Raft entries and Kafka offsets are not the same numbering space, offset_translator, L43 maps between them. Log compaction builds a compacted_index so key-based retention can rewrite segments without full scans, and small persistent bookkeeping lives in a RocksDB-backed kvstore, L93.

Thread-per-Core Sharding Explains the Throughput

Every component above is a Seastar shard-aware service — you can see the pattern in storage::api, L29 and the group and quota managers, all deriving from peering_sharded_service. There are no locks across cores: each shard exclusively owns the connections, Raft groups, and logs assigned to it, and cross-shard work happens through explicit message passing. This is the same philosophy that makes Redis fast, but applied to a replicated log: the Raft leader for a partition runs on one core, appends on that core, and replicates from that core, so the entire produce-to-disk path for a given partition is single-threaded by construction. Fewer synchronization primitives, predictable tail latencies, and performance that scales with core count rather than lock contention.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting a running broker is deliberately boring. On Debian/Ubuntu the README route is:

curl -1sLf 'https://linux.pkg.redpanda.com/setup-redpanda.deb.sh' | sudo -E bash
sudo apt-get install redpanda

Prefer building from source? The README documents a Bazel-based flow: install bazelisk, run sudo ./bazel/install-deps.sh, then bazel build --config=release //.... For a throwaway sandbox, rpk container start boots a broker in Docker (that is the macOS path in the README and it works anywhere Docker does).

Once the broker is up, exercise it the way an ML feature flow would — produce inference events, then consume them back:

rpk topic create inference-events
rpk topic produce inference-events -v \
  '{"model":"churn-v3","user":42,"score":0.87}'
rpk topic consume inference-events

Any standard Kafka client library — Python kafka-python, confluent-kafka, Spark Structured Streaming — connects the same way it would to Kafka, because the wire protocol handlers above are byte-compatible. Point your training job’s source at Redpanda and your serving loop’s sink at it too, and you have replayable data between them with no JVM in the middle.

Honest Limits

What this tour does not claim. We verified every file path and line number against the dev branch checkout at the time of writing; dev is Redpanda’s fast-moving development branch, so lines will drift and some cited code will be refactored. We read the README’s install and build instructions but did not execute them for this post, and we did not benchmark anything — throughput and latency claims you may have seen elsewhere are not repeated here because we could not reproduce them from source. The consumer-group-as-Raft-state-machine description rests on the class hierarchy we linked, not on an end-to-end trace. We also did not audit the transaction coordinator, tiered storage to S3-compatible object stores such as MinIO, or the newer “datalake” modules visible in the tree. Finally, the diagrams cover the raft, kafka, and storage trees we reviewed — the cluster manager, schema registry, and pandaproxy components are intentionally out of scope. Treat the diagrams as a map of the code we read, not a certification of production behavior — and if you deploy this for model feature serving, benchmark your own workload on your own hardware.
entry.summary: A guided source-code tour of Redpanda's Raft consensus layer, Kafka protocol server, and storage engine, with architecture diagrams linking straight into the C++ source.

entry.title: Inside RisingWave: A Source Tour of the Rust Streaming Database Powering Always-Fresh Features

link.title: Inside RisingWave: A Source Tour of the Rust Streaming Database Powering Always-Fresh Features

entry.content:
If you build AI systems, you eventually hit the same wall: your model was trained on a snapshot, but the world kept moving. Feature vectors go stale, dashboards lag, retrieval indexes drift. RisingWave attacks that problem from the database side. It is a Postgres-compatible streaming database written in Rust: you declare a SQL materialized view over an event stream, and it maintains that view incrementally as data arrives. There is no “refresh” step and no batch job. For ML infrastructure, that makes a materialized view an ideal feature table — always fresh, queryable over the Postgres wire protocol, and cheap to serve straight into model inference.

What makes the project worth a source tour is that almost none of that is magic glue over existing engines. The query plans compile into a distributed dataflow of actors, the state lives in a custom LSM-style store called Hummock that treats S3-compatible object storage as the source of truth, and a single elected meta service coordinates everything. The README is blunt about the ambition: replace the Debezium + Kafka + Flink + serving-database chain with one system that ingests, processes, and serves.

In this tour we walk the main branch of risingwavelabs/risingwave through two diagrams — a wide overview, then a deeper pass across the three pillars: the streaming DAG, the state store, and the meta service. Every symbol cited below was verified against the actual source tree.

Figure 1 — RisingWave overview: the meta control plane assigns work, compute nodes run actor DAGs, and Hummock keeps state on object storage.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The process entry point is compute_node_serve, L93, which wires a compute node’s stream manager, batch engine, and barrier worker together, then registers with the meta node.
  • On the control plane, rpc_serve, L127 exposes the meta services, while start_service_as_election_leader, L317 shows the elected-leader model the whole system leans on.
  • DDL flows into DdlController, L282, which turns a CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW into a streaming job.
  • Fragment placement happens in GlobalStreamManager, L346, which broadcasts fragments to every compute node.
  • On each node, LocalStreamManager, L67 materializes those fragments into runnable actors.
  • Checkpointing is pushed by GlobalBarrierManager, L47 and mirrored locally by LocalBarrierManager, L106.
  • State flows through LocalHummockStorage, L63, the per-node implementation of the state store that backs everything with object storage.

Figure 2 — The detail view: barrier commands, actor exchange, executor state tables, and the Hummock flush/compaction loop.

The Streaming DAG: Actors, Fragments, Executors

RisingWave’s unit of parallelism is the actor: one shard of one fragment, running an executor chain as a stream of messages. The interesting design choice is in src/stream/src/executor/mod.rs: the Execute, L246 trait has a single method that consumes the executor and returns a BoxedMessageStream, and the runtime-facing Executor, L259 is a small struct pairing that box with schema metadata. Every operator — joins, aggregations, windows — is just a Rust stream transformation, which keeps the code surprisingly flat.

Data and control share the same channel by design. A Barrier, L413 is a message that flows through the DAG exactly like a data chunk, carrying a two-part epoch plus an optional Mutation, L362 — the mechanism used to add or drop upstreams during scaling and recovery. Because barriers align at every join point, reaching the next epoch downstream means the whole fragment is consistent, which is what makes “materialized view” a promise rather than a hope.

The operators themselves read like a Flink catalog written by database people. HashAggExecutor, L64 maintains grouped state incrementally, HashJoinExecutor, L158 keeps both sides’ materialized inputs, and MaterializeExecutor, L68 is the endpoint that writes an upstream changelog into the table backing your view. Ingestion enters via SourceExecutor, L100, and results leave through SinkExecutor, L57. Between fragments, DispatchExecutor, L62 fans output out through a HashDataDispatcher, L885 that routes rows by key, while RemoteInput, L146 and Output, L27 handle the gRPC exchange across nodes.

All executor state goes through one abstraction: StateTable, L258, a typed key-value wrapper that knows about virtual nodes, epochs, and serialization. That uniform interface is what lets the storage layer below evolve without touching operators.

Concretely, Actor::run, L228 is the pump: it polls the executor’s message stream, negotiates barrier alignment at merge points, and forwards data only after control messages have been observed. Evaluation errors are not swallowed either — they surface through the ActorEvalErrorReport, L79 hook in the local stream manager, so a poison row becomes a visible, attributable failure instead of a silently stuck fragment.

Hummock: An LSM State Store That Lives on S3

Hummock is RisingWave’s answer to a question most stream processors punt on: where does state live if a node dies? The answer is “object storage, first-class.” Writes land in an in-memory shared buffer — see SharedBufferBatch, L204 — where they are immediately readable before being flushed. An event-driven uploader converts buffered writes into immutable SSTables; the handoff runs through HummockEventSender, L133, and the encoding happens in SstableBuilder, L136, which packs sorted keys into blocks with bloom-style filters. The SstableStore, L206 abstracts the actual file placement, so S3, MinIO, or a local disk are configuration rather than code.

Reads merge those layers lazily. MergeIterator, L62 implements the k-way merge across memtable contents and every relevant SSTable level, ordering by user key and collapsing versions by epoch. Because each read is pinned to a specific version — the HummockVersion, L235 type records which SSTable levels are visible at which epoch — snapshots are essentially free, and a query against a two-minute-old epoch reads exactly the files that were current then. On top of that, the store layers a block cache and recent-write filters (both live in the same hummock module tree), so repeated feature lookups — the classic online-inference access pattern — mostly avoid touching network storage at all.

Compaction closes the loop. CompactorRunner, L70 executes merge tasks that rewrite key ranges into fewer, larger SSTables, dropping superseded versions as it goes. Version metadata about those files is tracked separately and served by the meta service, so a recovered compute node can re-pin state from scratch without shipping its old disks along. A batch-query-facing sibling, HummockStorage, L96, shares all of this machinery so that SQL reads against your views hit the same store the actors write to.

For feature-serving workloads this shape matters more than the internals: feature tables become cheap to keep large, because hot keys sit in memory or local cache while cold history costs object-storage prices instead of RAM prices.

The Meta Service: One Elected Brain

Everything global lives behind the meta node. src/meta/node/src/server.rs starts the gRPC surface with an election-aware split between leader and follower serving, and the plan-to-actors translation is owned by ActorGraphBuilder, L438, which turns a logical stream plan into per-actor graphs with parallelism and dispatchers decided up front.

The barrier path is the most consequential piece of the control plane. GlobalBarrierWorker, L85 runs on the elected leader, drives each Command, L465 to completion across all actors, and only then commits the corresponding storage version. Checkpoint interval becomes a tuning knob between latency and recovery cost, not a correctness cliff. Storage metadata gets symmetric treatment in HummockManager, L155, which commits SSTable manifests and versions, and CompactorManager, L411, which routes compaction tasks to registered workers.

You can watch the whole system’s health from outside: RisingWave exports Prometheus metrics throughout the executor layer, and our Prometheus tour covers the scrape side. The same executor plumbing pairs naturally with a Kafka source (source tour) or its lighter cousin Redpanda (sibling post) feeding CDC events into the DAG, while MinIO (source tour) is a common S3-compatible backend for Hummock in self-hosted setups. Each of these is configuration, not code: the connector layer resolves split assignments, and the barrier machinery we just walked keeps every integration consistent.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest path is the official Docker quickstart, which starts a single-node RisingWave and connects with psql over the Postgres wire protocol:

docker run -it --pull=always -p 4566:4566 risingwavelabs/risingwave:latest \
  psql -h localhost -p 4566 -d dev -U root

Now create a streaming source and a materialized view — here with the built-in datagen connector so the demo runs without external infrastructure:

CREATE SOURCE page_visits (
  user_id BIGINT,
  url VARCHAR,
  ts TIMESTAMP
) WITH (
  connector = 'datagen',
  fields.user_id.min = '1',
  fields.user_id.max = '1000'
) FORMAT PLAIN ENCODE JSON;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW user_visit_counts AS
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS visits, MAX(ts) AS last_seen
FROM page_visits
GROUP BY user_id;

SELECT * FROM user_visit_counts WHERE user_id = 42;

Run the SELECT twice and you will see different numbers: no refresh command exists because the view is maintained continuously. The single container is only a sandbox — for anything real, the project’s Docker Compose path separates meta, compute, and compactor processes so compute scales horizontally, with the control plane we walked above handling placement and rescheduling.

To turn this into a feature table for a Python model, replace datagen with a Kafka or Redpanda connector reading CDC events, then point your serving script at the view over the Postgres protocol. Any pandas.read_sql or asyncpg call against user_visit_counts now reads features that are current to within your checkpoint interval — and the same view is also a sink target if you need to stream features onward into a feature store or vector index.

Honest Limits

Everything above is verified by reading main at commit time, but scope matters. The performance characteristics here are architectural, not benchmarked: we did not run latency or throughput measurements, and the README’s claims about replacing the Flink stack are the project’s own positioning. Single-node Docker is a demo configuration — production deployments run separate meta, compute, and compactor processes with real etcd-style coordination concerns around the elected leader. SQL coverage is Postgres-compatible rather than Postgres-complete; exotic extensions, triggers, and stored procedures are not the point of a streaming engine, and some frontend features are still evolving on main. Finally, Hummock’s object-storage-first design optimizes for elasticity and recovery over single-digit-millisecond point reads; latency-sensitive paths lean on the disk cache documented by the project rather than on magic. Read the source — it is genuinely readable — before betting an SLA on it.
entry.summary: How RisingWave turns SQL materialized views into a distributed streaming DAG backed by the Hummock state store on object storage — traced through the Rust source.

entry.title: Inside Argo CD’s Source: How the GitOps Controller Turns Git Commits into Cluster State

link.title: Inside Argo CD’s Source: How the GitOps Controller Turns Git Commits into Cluster State

entry.content:
GitOps is the operating model where Git is the source of truth for what runs in your cluster, and a controller’s only job is to close the loop between the repository and the API server. For AI/ML infrastructure this matters more than almost anywhere else. Model serving stacks are stacks of YAML: a Kubernetes Deployment for the inference server, a Service and Ingress in front of it, and a PVC or object-store credential Secret behind it. When a new model checkpoint passes evaluation, the “promotion” step should not be a human typing kubectl apply at 2 a.m. — it should be a commit to a Git repo that a machine reconciles faithfully.

Argo CD is the most widely deployed implementation of that idea. It is a Kubernetes controller written in Go (CNCF graduated, packaged with Helm charts), and it watches custom resources called Applications. Each Application declares two halves: a source (a Git repo, revision and path) and a destination (a cluster and namespace). Argo CD continuously renders the manifests from Git, diffs them against what actually exists in the destination cluster, and reports or corrects the drift. The same contract works for a five-file demo and for a fleet-wide model rollout, which is why ML platform teams adopt it for promotion between staging and production.

This post is a source tour of the three main components — the application controller, the repo-server render service, and the API server — based on the code at master (fresh sparse checkout). Two architecture diagrams generated from the source tree anchor the discussion; every file path and symbol below was grepped and line-checked against that checkout.

Overview: the API server fronts users, the repo-server renders Git into manifests, and the application controller diffs and syncs them into target clusters, sharing a Redis cache and a Kubernetes-backed configuration store.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Git repository — the declarative source of truth. Nothing in Argo CD mutates Git; it only reads it, which is why commits are the promotion unit for model rollouts.
  • Repo server — a stateless gRPC render service, started by NewServer, L49. It clones repositories, checks out revisions and turns Helm charts, Kustomize overlays or raw YAML into a flat list of manifests.
  • API server — the gateway for the UI, CLI and CI systems, assembled in NewServer, L331. It handles auth, RBAC and Application CRUD, and serves a watch stream via Watch, L1266.
  • Application controller — the reconciliation brain, started by Run, L930 with separate worker pools for status refreshes, operations and hydration.
  • App state manager — the comparison half, CompareAppState, L682, which produces the diff between rendered target state and live objects.
  • Sync engine — the acting half, SyncAppState, L160, which applies, prunes and waits across sync waves.
  • Shared infrastructure — the Redis-backed cache in NewCache, L46 and the configuration store NewDB, L134, which persists clusters and repo credentials as Kubernetes Secrets.
  • Target clusters — where the work lands; every managed object gets tracking applied by SetAppInstanceLabel, L23 so Argo CD knows which Application owns it.

Detail view: the refresh queue feeds CompareAppState, the operation queue feeds SyncAppState, and both lean on the repo-server, the cluster store and the shared caches.

The Reconciliation Loop

The controller’s main loop lives in controller/appcontroller.go. Run, L930 starts three worker pools: status processors drain the refresh queue, operation processors drain the operation queue, and hydration processors handle the source-hydrator flow. Each status worker runs processAppRefreshQueueItem, L2125: it pops an Application from the queue, checks project locks, then asks the app state manager to compare.

Comparison is the heart of the loop. CompareAppState, L682 first calls GetRepoObjs, L229 to fetch rendered manifests from the repo-server, then NormalizeTargetObjects, L574 stamps tracking identity and strips noise so diffs stay clean. Live state comes from informer caches per cluster, and the result carries both sync status and health. Health itself is aggregated by setApplicationHealth, L25, which honors per-resource Lua overrides. Each successful comparison is recorded by persistRevisionHistory, L1268, which is what makes later rollbacks possible.

If the application’s sync policy is automated and status is OutOfSync, the refresh path calls autoSync, L2830 to create a sync operation — that is the self-healing behavior that reverts a manual kubectl edit minutes after it happens. Operations are consumed by processAppOperationQueueItem, L1057, which delegates to the sync engine. Separately, Run, L56 keeps the cluster cache fresh with API counts so the UI can show cluster load.

Rendering Manifests in the Repo Server

The repo-server is deliberately stateless so it scales horizontally. GenerateManifest, L667 is the entry RPC the controller and API server call. On a cache miss it proceeds to runManifestGen, L847, which needs an actual working tree: checkoutRevision, L3131 pins the exact commit, including submodules, before any template engine runs.

The underlying Git plumbing is in util/git/client.go. Fetch, L720 retrieves objects with retry, and Checkout, L814 resolves the revision and updates the working copy. Because rendering depends on Helm and Kustomize binaries, the repo-server image bundles those tools; the manifest cache lives in the shared Redis tier so multiple replicas answer consistently. For UI parameter editing, GetAppDetails, L2555 exposes Helm values and Kustomize images without a full render.

The Sync Engine, Waves and Hooks

Syncing is not one apply. SyncAppState, L160 groups resources into sync waves and phases (PreSync, Sync, PostSync), waits between waves, and honors maintenance windows through syncWindowPreventsSync, L730. Hooks — Jobs that must complete before traffic shifts, like an eval harness validating a model before it serves — are orchestrated in the same state machine. Per-resource outcomes are seeded by newSyncOperationResult, L137 and written back into the Application’s operationState, so progress is visible in real time in the UI.

For an ML platform this phasing is exactly what a canary model promotion needs: PreSync runs the dataset validation job, the wave containing the new Deployment applies, and PostSync flips the Helm values or traffic weights only after the readiness gates pass.

The API Server Surface

Everything users touch flows through server/server.go. NewServer, L331 wires the service set, RBAC enforcer, OIDC/Dex session management and settings watchers, then Run, L598 serves a gRPC listener and an HTTP gateway built by newHTTPServer, L1247 for gRPC-Web, Swagger and health endpoints. The application package implements the gRPC surface: Get, L792 reads from informer caches rather than hitting etcd directly, and Sync, L2120 validates RBAC and sync options, resolves source revisions, then writes the operation onto the Application resource — the controller picks it up from its watch, so API server and controller never call each other directly. Cluster and repository credentials live behind ListClusters, L73 in the Secret-backed store, keeping etcd as the only database.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting from zero to a synced Application takes three steps. First, install: apply the Argo CD manifests (kubectl create namespace argocd, then kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml), or install through the official Helm chart. You get the three components from this tour, a Redis instance, and a repo-server with Helm/Kustomize available inside. For a cluster already running containerd-based Kubernetes nodes, no special host setup is required — Argo CD is a normal set of controller pods.

Second, connect a repository. Push your model-serving manifests (the inference Deployment, Service, and a ConfigMap with model version) into a Git repo, then either register it in the UI/CLI (argocd repo add) or rely on credentials stored in the Secret-backed config store.

Third, create and sync an Application:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: llm-serving
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://git.example.com/ml/platform.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: overlays/prod
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: serving
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: false
      selfHeal: true

Apply that with kubectl, and the controller reconciles it: the repo-server renders overlays/prod, CompareAppState diffs against live state, and with automated enabled the sync engine applies the result. Promoting a new model version becomes a Git commit; the controller does the rest, and selfHeal reverts any out-of-band cluster changes.

Honest Limits

Everything above comes from the source and README of the current master tree — no benchmarks were invented here. A few caveats. The diagrams are hand-authored simplifications built from the file tree; they show component relationships, not every call path. The source tour reflects master at the time of writing, and this codebase moves fast — line numbers cited (like GenerateManifest, L667) will shift as the code evolves, though the symbol names are stable. ApplicationSets and the notification controller live in the repository but outside the four directories examined here, so they are not covered. Performance characteristics — render latency, reconciliation throughput, cache hit rates — depend on repository size, cluster count and resource volume; nothing here is a benchmark. Finally, GitOps removes manual drift, not misconfigurations: a bad commit syncs just as faithfully as a good one, so review gates and sync windows still matter.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of Argo CD showing how the application controller, repo-server render service and API server cooperate to sync Git into Kubernetes clusters.

entry.title: containerd Source Tour: The Daemon, the Shim Protocol, and the Snapshot Layer

link.title: containerd Source Tour: The Daemon, the Shim Protocol, and the Snapshot Layer

entry.content:
Every AI inference service you deploy — a Triton server, a vLLM worker, or a plain FastAPI wrapper around a fine-tuned model — exists as a container on some Linux host.
